title: Emotion, Reward and Motivation
summary: How limbic and neuromodulatory circuits generate feelings, learn value and drive behavior.

lessons.title: The Amygdala and Fear Conditioning

levels.kid:
Deep inside your brain, on each side, sits a small part shaped like an almond. It is called the **amygdala** (say: uh-MIG-duh-luh). Its job is to spot danger fast, like a smoke alarm.

Scientists study it with a simple experiment. A rat hears a beep. Right after, it feels a small zap on its feet. After this happens a few times, the rat hears the beep alone and stays very still. That stillness is called **freezing**. The rat has learned that the beep means "danger is coming."

This kind of learning is called **fear conditioning**. The amygdala is where the beep and the zap get linked together.

Your amygdala helps keep you safe, too. It is why you jump back from something that looks like a snake, even before you think!
levels.hs:
The **amygdala** is an almond-shaped cluster of nuclei in the medial temporal lobe, one in each hemisphere, just in front of the hippocampus. It is the brain's best-studied hub for detecting threats and learning what predicts them.

The classic experiment is **Pavlovian fear conditioning**:
- A neutral **conditioned stimulus (CS)**, such as a tone, is paired with an **unconditioned stimulus (US)**, such as a mild foot shock.
- After a few pairings, the tone alone triggers a **conditioned response (CR)**: freezing, a racing heart and a stronger startle reflex.

Two regions of the amygdala matter most:
- The **lateral nucleus** receives sensory information. This is where the tone and shock signals meet and become linked.
- The **central nucleus** is the output hub. It sends commands to the brainstem and hypothalamus that produce the body's fear responses.

Neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux described a fast **"low road"** running from the thalamus straight to the amygdala, and a slower, more detailed **"high road"** that passes through the cortex first. The low road lets you flinch at a stick before you realize it isn't a snake.

Humans show the same pattern. A woman known as **patient S.M.** has **Urbach-Wiethe disease**, a rare condition that destroyed both of her amygdalae. She shows almost no fear in situations that frighten most people and has trouble recognizing fear in other people's faces.
levels.college:
Fear conditioning is a powerful model because it is fast, often a single trial is enough, it is conserved from rodents to humans, and its circuit is well mapped.

**Inputs.** Auditory CS information reaches the **lateral amygdala (LA)** through two routes: directly from the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and indirectly through auditory cortex. Nociceptive US information also converges on LA. Lesions of LA, but not of auditory cortex alone, block conditioning to a simple tone.

**Plasticity.** Learning depends on strengthening the CS-to-LA synapses:
- When CS input arrives as the US strongly depolarizes LA neurons, **NMDA receptors** detect the coincidence, and the resulting calcium influx triggers **long-term potentiation (LTP)**.
- Infusing an NMDA antagonist into the amygdala during training blocks acquisition of fear.
- Turning the short-term change into a long-term memory requires PKA, MAPK/ERK signaling, the transcription factor **CREB** and new protein synthesis.

**Intrinsic circuit and outputs.** LA projects to the basal nucleus (together these form the **basolateral complex**, BLA) and to the **central nucleus (CeA)**. CeA drives the responses:
- **Ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (PAG)**: freezing
- **Lateral hypothalamus**: sympathetic arousal (heart rate, blood pressure)
- **Paraventricular hypothalamus**: stress hormone release
- **Brainstem nuclei**: potentiated startle, respiration

**Context.** Rats also fear the chamber where shock happened. Contextual fear requires the **hippocampus**: hippocampal lesions made shortly after training (Kim and Fanselow, 1992) abolish fear of the context but spare fear of the tone.

**Human evidence.** In fMRI, the amygdala activates to a CS early in conditioning. Bechara and colleagues (1995) found a double dissociation. A patient with amygdala damage lacked a conditioned skin conductance (sweat) response but could state which tone predicted the loud noise. A patient with hippocampal damage showed the reverse.
levels.phd:
Modern work resolves the amygdala into cell-type-specific microcircuits.

**Hebbian plus modulatory learning.** Conditioning potentiates thalamic and cortical inputs to LA. Rogan, Stäubli and LeDoux (1997) showed CS-evoked field potentials in LA grow with learning, and McKernan and Shinnick-Gallagher (1997) found occluded LTP in slices from conditioned rats. Johansen and colleagues (2010) showed that pairing a tone with optogenetic depolarization of LA pyramidal neurons, in place of a shock, produces conditioned fear. Pure postsynaptic depolarization is not always sufficient, however: later work (Johansen et al., 2014) indicated that coincident neuromodulatory signals, notably beta-adrenergic, are needed to stabilize Hebbian plasticity.

**Memory allocation.** Which LA neurons join the engram is competitive. Josselyn, Silva and colleagues (Han et al., 2007, 2009) showed that neurons overexpressing CREB, which are more excitable, are preferentially recruited. Ablating those neurons with diphtheria toxin after training selectively erased the memory.

**CeA microcircuitry.** The lateral subdivision (CeL) contains mutually inhibitory GABAergic populations. **PKC-delta-positive (CeL-off)** neurons tonically inhibit medial CeA (CeM) output neurons. **Somatostatin-positive (CeL-on)** neurons, which are potentiated by conditioning (Li et al., 2013), inhibit PKC-delta cells. The CS therefore disinhibits CeM, which drives PAG and freezing (Haubensak et al., 2010; Ciocchi et al., 2010). **Intercalated cell** clusters provide further gating between BLA and CeA.

**Beyond fear.** The amygdala encodes valence, not just threat. Paton, Salzman and colleagues (2006) found BLA neurons tracking positive or negative value of the same cue. Namburi, Tye and colleagues (2015) showed that BLA projections to nucleus accumbens favor reward learning, whereas projections to CeA favor aversive learning. Kim and Tonegawa (2016) identified genetically distinct BLA populations for each.

**Controversy.** LeDoux's **two-system framework** argues that the amygdala drives defensive survival circuits, while the conscious feeling of fear arises from cortical networks. On this view, freezing in a rat is not evidence of subjective fear, and fear conditioning should be called **threat conditioning**. Others counter that the amygdala contributes to emotional experience too.
levels.expert:
Fear conditioning is the main laboratory bridge between rodent circuits and human anxiety disorders, but translation has pitfalls.

**Human lesion nuances.** S.M. does not fear snakes, spiders or horror films, and she fails to fixate the eye region of faces (Adolphs et al., 2005), which partly explains her poor recognition of fear. Yet Feinstein and colleagues (2013) found that she and two other Urbach-Wiethe patients experienced intense panic when inhaling carbon dioxide. Interoceptive threats can therefore generate fear through brainstem and other extra-amygdala routes. The amygdala seems critical for fear evoked by external cues, not for all fear.

**Measurement pitfalls.**
- Freezing is not the only defensive response. Gruene, Shansky and colleagues (2015) found that many female rats "dart" instead, so freezing-only scoring misclassified them as poor learners.
- Fanselow's **threat imminence** model shows that defensive behavior changes with distance from the threat: vigilance, then freezing, then flight.
- Human amygdala fMRI suffers susceptibility artifacts and draining-vein contamination, and responses habituate rapidly across trials.

**Clinical links.** PTSD and anxiety disorders show heightened amygdala reactivity and **overgeneralization**, meaning fear spreads to cues that merely resemble the CS (Lissek). Noradrenaline acting at BLA beta receptors strengthens consolidation of emotional memories (McGaugh). This motivated studies of propranolol after trauma, with mixed results.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** The amygdala is a frequent seizure focus in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, and fear or a rising epigastric sensation can be an aura. Stereo-EEG stimulation of the amygdala elicits fear inconsistently and can produce other emotions or none. Selective amygdalohippocampectomy and laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) remove or ablate it. Brief direct stimulation has enhanced later recognition memory without awareness (Inman et al., 2018). Amygdala deep brain stimulation for refractory PTSD remains at the stage of small early trials.

**Open questions.** How do BLA engrams interact with prefrontal and hippocampal representations in humans? Are threat-conditioning deficits a cause of anxiety disorders or a consequence of them? Can cell-type-specific CeA targeting become feasible therapeutically?

keyPoints: The amygdala is a set of nuclei in the medial temporal lobe that detects threat
Fear conditioning pairs a neutral CS (tone) with an aversive US (shock)
The lateral nucleus links CS and US through NMDA-dependent LTP
The central nucleus drives freezing (via PAG) and autonomic responses
The hippocampus is needed for fear of a context, not of a simple tone
Patient S.M. shows the amygdala is key for fear of external threats

test.q: In fear conditioning, a tone that comes to predict a shock is called the:
test.explain: The tone starts out neutral and becomes meaningful through pairing, so it is the conditioned stimulus. The shock is the unconditioned stimulus.

test.q: Which amygdala nucleus is the main site where tone and shock signals converge?
test.explain: The lateral nucleus receives sensory inputs, where CS and US signals meet and become linked. The central nucleus is the output hub.

test.q: What is the main role of the central nucleus of the amygdala in fear?
test.explain: The central nucleus projects to the PAG, hypothalamus and brainstem to produce freezing and autonomic changes.

test.q: Freezing in a fear-conditioned rat depends on central amygdala projections to the:
test.explain: The ventrolateral periaqueductal gray produces freezing. The other structures are not the CeA output for this response.

test.q: LeDoux's fast 'low road' for threat signals runs:
test.explain: The low road carries crude sensory information from the thalamus straight to the amygdala. The high road passes through cortex first.

test.q: Rats given hippocampal lesions shortly after conditioning lose their fear of:
test.explain: Contextual fear needs the hippocampus, while fear of a simple tone relies on the amygdala and is spared (Kim and Fanselow, 1992).

test.q: Infusing an NMDA receptor antagonist into the amygdala during training most likely:
choices: Makes the shock itself less painful
Speeds up later loss of the fear
test.explain: NMDA receptors detect CS-US coincidence and trigger LTP in the lateral amygdala, so blocking them prevents acquisition.

test.q: Patient S.M. lost both amygdalae because of which disease?
test.explain: Urbach-Wiethe disease can calcify and destroy the amygdalae bilaterally, leaving S.M. with little fear of external threats.

test.q: In Bechara's 1995 study, the patient with amygdala damage:
choices: Showed a normal response and normal memory
Had a sweat response but forgot the pairing
Lacked a sweat response but knew the pairing
Lost the sweat response and the memory too
test.explain: The amygdala patient had no conditioned skin conductance response but could report the contingency. The hippocampal patient showed the reverse.

test.q: What defensive behavior, standing completely motionless, is the classic measure of conditioned fear in rodents?
test.explain: Freezing, the absence of all movement except breathing, is the standard readout of fear in rats and mice.

test.q: The amygdala is an almond-shaped group of nuclei in the medial ___ lobe.
test.explain: It sits deep in the medial temporal lobe, just in front of the hippocampus.

test.q: The lateral and basal nuclei together form the ___ complex of the amygdala.
test.explain: The basolateral complex (BLA) is the main input and learning region, which projects to the central nucleus.

kidTest.q: Where is the amygdala?
kidTest.explain: The amygdala is a small part deep inside the brain, one on each side.

kidTest.q: What shape is the amygdala?
kidTest.explain: Its name comes from the Greek word for almond. The seahorse-shaped part nearby is the hippocampus.

kidTest.q: In the experiment, what does the rat learn the beep means?
kidTest.explain: The beep came right before a small zap, so the rat learns the beep predicts danger.

kidTest.q: What is the amygdala's main job?
kidTest.explain: Like a smoke alarm, the amygdala spots danger quickly.

kidTest.q: When a scared rat stays very, very still, we call it f _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Staying still is called freezing. It is how rats show they are afraid.

advancedTest.q: If somatostatin-positive (CeL-on) neurons are silenced during the CS, the expected effect on freezing is:
choices: Increased, via direct lateral amygdala output to PAG
Increased, as CeM output loses its tonic inhibition
Reduced, as PKC-delta cells inhibit CeM output more
Unchanged, as CeL cells send no onward projections
advancedTest.explain: SOM+ cells normally inhibit PKC-delta cells, which tonically inhibit CeM. Silencing SOM+ cells releases PKC-delta inhibition onto CeM, reducing the output that drives PAG and freezing.

advancedTest.q: A patient with selective bilateral hippocampal damage undergoes tone-noise conditioning. The most likely result is:
choices: No conditioned response and an accurate account of the pairing
No conditioned response and no account of the pairing either
A conditioned response but no account of the pairing
A normal conditioned response and accurate pairing recall
advancedTest.explain: Bechara's double dissociation showed that the intact amygdala supports the conditioned skin conductance response, while hippocampal damage impairs declarative knowledge of the contingency.

advancedTest.q: Pairing a tone with optogenetic depolarization of lateral amygdala pyramidal neurons, with no shock, produces conditioned fear. This mainly shows that:
choices: Tone memories are stored in the hippocampus
The PAG is unnecessary for freezing behavior
Pain awareness is needed for fear learning
LA depolarization can stand in for the shock
advancedTest.explain: The artificial depolarization substituted for the US, supporting a Hebbian model at CS-to-LA synapses. It does not test the PAG, and it argues against needing conscious pain.

advancedTest.q: S.M. shows little fear of external threats yet panics when inhaling carbon dioxide. The best interpretation is that:
choices: Her fear of outside cues was merely suppressed
Carbon dioxide acts mainly on the lateral nucleus
Her remaining amygdala tissue recovered with age
Internal threat signals can evoke fear without it
advancedTest.explain: Interoceptive threats such as rising carbon dioxide can trigger fear through brainstem and other routes, so the amygdala is critical for externally cued fear but not for all fear.

lessons.title: Extinction, Reconsolidation and Updating Emotional Memories

levels.kid:
Imagine a dog barked at you once at the park. Now every time you see that park, your tummy feels tight. Your brain learned: park means scary.

But what if you go back again and again, and nothing bad happens? Slowly the scary feeling fades. Scientists call this **extinction**. The old scary memory is not erased. Your brain writes a new note on top that says, "Park is safe now."

Sometimes the old fear sneaks back, like after a long time away. That shows the first note was still there.

Scientists also found that when you remember something, the memory gets soft for a little while, like clay. During that time, it can be changed before it hardens again.
levels.hs:
In fear conditioning, the brain links a neutral cue (a tone) with something unpleasant (a mild shock), so the cue alone triggers fear. But fears can be updated in two main ways.

**Extinction** happens when the cue is shown many times without the bad outcome. Fear responses drop. Importantly, extinction is **new learning**, not erasing. The original memory survives, which explains three classic findings:
- **Spontaneous recovery**: fear returns after time passes.
- **Renewal**: fear returns in a different place (context) than where extinction happened.
- **Reinstatement**: fear returns after an unexpected unpleasant event.

The **prefrontal cortex**, especially a region at the front and middle of the brain, helps hold the "it's safe now" memory and calm the **amygdala**, the brain's threat detector.

**Reconsolidation** is a different idea. When a stored memory is recalled, it can briefly become unstable and must be re-stored. During this window, the memory may be strengthened, weakened or edited.

Real example: **exposure therapy** for phobias and PTSD works much like extinction. A person with a spider phobia gradually faces spiders safely until fear falls. Because the old fear memory still exists, therapists practice in many settings to prevent relapse.
levels.college:
Emotional memories are not fixed records. Two processes allow updating: **extinction**, which adds a competing memory, and **reconsolidation**, which may modify the original trace.

**Extinction circuitry** (mostly rodent work):
- Repeated CS-alone trials create a CS-no US association.
- **Infralimbic cortex (IL)**, analogous to human **ventromedial PFC (vmPFC)**, drives inhibitory **intercalated cells** and other inhibitory cells in the amygdala, damping output from the central nucleus.
- **Prelimbic cortex (PL)**, analogous to human dorsal anterior cingulate, tends to promote fear expression.
- The **hippocampus** encodes context, gating which memory wins. That explains **renewal** (ABA design: conditioned in A, extinguished in B, tested in A).
- Extinction consolidation needs **NMDA receptors**; blocking them impairs it, while the partial NMDA agonist **D-cycloserine** enhanced extinction in rats.

**Reconsolidation**:
- A consolidated memory, when reactivated, becomes **labile** and needs new **protein synthesis** to restabilize.
- Nader, Schafe and LeDoux (2000) infused the protein-synthesis inhibitor **anisomycin** into the lateral amygdala right after a reminder tone; rats later showed reduced fear. Without reactivation, anisomycin had no effect.
- The labile window lasts roughly a few hours.

**Key differences**:
- Extinction: many unreinforced trials; original memory intact; fear can return.
- Reconsolidation blockade: brief reactivation; claimed to weaken the original trace, with less return of fear.

**Boundary conditions** limit reconsolidation. Older, stronger memories resist it, and too long a reminder shifts the brain toward extinction. **Prediction error**, a mismatch between expectation and outcome, appears necessary to destabilize a memory. This is why researchers are interested in reconsolidation-based therapies.
levels.phd:
Extinction is an inhibitory association layered over an intact CS-US trace, as shown by renewal, reinstatement and spontaneous recovery (Bouton). Its neural substrate is a distributed loop. During extinction learning, BLA "extinction neurons" (Herry et al., 2008) increase firing while "fear neurons" decrease, with connectivity to mPFC differing between the populations. IL activity and burst firing during recall predict extinction retrieval (Milad and Quirk, 2002). IL stimulation mimics extinction, and IL inactivation impairs recall. Downstream, IL engages intercalated cells and inhibitory interneurons in BLA, suppressing CeM output to periaqueductal gray and hypothalamus. Ventral hippocampal projections to IL and PL gate context dependence. Molecularly, extinction consolidation requires NMDA receptors, BDNF in IL, and MAPK signaling, and endocannabinoid (CB1) signaling supports it.

Reconsolidation revived Misanin's 1968 observation. Nader et al. (2000) showed that post-retrieval intra-LA anisomycin abolished long-term but not short-term fear memory, a signature of restabilization failure. Destabilization requires **GluN2B**-containing NMDA receptors and proteasome-dependent protein degradation. Restabilization requires GluN2A and new protein synthesis, plus **β-adrenergic** signaling. This motivated **propranolol** studies: Kindt et al. (2009) gave propranolol before reactivation in humans and erased the fear-potentiated startle while leaving declarative knowledge of the CS-US contingency intact.

A behavioral variant, **retrieval-extinction** (Monfils et al., 2009; Schiller et al., 2010), places extinction within the reconsolidation window after a single reminder. This reduced spontaneous recovery and renewal, sometimes for a year in humans, and linked to removal of calcium-permeable (GluA2-lacking) AMPA receptors in LA.

Controversies remain. Prediction error is required for destabilization, but the right amount is narrow. Too little leaves the memory stable, while too much triggers new extinction learning, creating a "limbo" zone (Sevenster). Several replication attempts of retrieval-extinction and propranolol effects failed. Debates also persist over whether reconsolidation blockade truly erases memory or produces retrieval failure. Spontaneous recovery after some amnesic manipulations argues for retrieval accounts.
levels.expert:
Clinically, extinction maps onto **exposure therapy**, the most robustly supported treatment for anxiety disorders, OCD and PTSD. Translation exposed failure modes. Patients with PTSD show impaired extinction recall with lower vmPFC and higher dACC and amygdala activity (Milad et al., 2009). It remains unresolved whether this is a pre-existing vulnerability or a consequence of trauma.

Michelle Craske's **inhibitory learning** framework reshaped exposure practice. It emphasizes how strongly the safety learning is retrievable, not how fast fear falls within a session:
- **Expectancy violation**: design exposures to maximize mismatch with the feared outcome, a prediction-error principle.
- **Variability and multiple contexts** reduce renewal.
- **Deepened extinction**: combine cues, and test retrieval cues.
- Remove **safety behaviors**, which prevent disconfirmation.

Pharmacological augmentation has been sobering. D-cycloserine meta-analyses (Mataix-Cols et al., 2017) showed small effects at best. It may enhance whatever was learned, including a bad session, so timing after successful exposure matters. Glucocorticoids, yohimbine and methylene blue have been studied as enhancers, with mixed results. MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD has been framed as enhancing extinction or reconsolidation, but the FDA rejected the application in 2024 amid concerns about functional unblinding and data quality.

Reconsolidation-based treatment: Brunet and colleagues' propranolol-with-reactivation approach showed PTSD symptom reductions in open and some randomized trials. Rigorous controlled replication is limited, and memory age and strength remain boundary conditions. Soeter and Kindt reported reduced spider-phobia avoidance after a single reactivation plus propranolol. Pitfalls include the absence of a reliable biomarker telling you a memory was actually destabilized, and the risk of strengthening it instead.

Frontier directions include:
- **Engram** work (Tonegawa, Josselyn) that tags and reactivates the specific cell ensembles active during learning. These experiments show extinction recruits partially distinct ensembles, and that suppressed fear engrams persist.
- Memory **updating in sleep** and targeted memory reactivation.
- Ethical questions around "editing" emotional memory, including identity and legal testimony concerns.

For surgery-minded learners, vmPFC and amygdala lesion data, together with deep brain stimulation trials in refractory PTSD, link this circuit to neuromodulation.

Open questions include separating true erasure from retrieval failure, and predicting individual destabilization windows.

keyPoints: Extinction is new safety learning layered on top of an intact fear memory
Spontaneous recovery, renewal and reinstatement show the old memory survives
vmPFC/infralimbic cortex and hippocampus regulate the amygdala during extinction
Reactivated memories become labile and need protein synthesis to reconsolidate
Prediction error is needed to destabilize a memory; boundary conditions limit effects
Exposure therapy uses extinction; reconsolidation therapies remain under study

test.q: Fear extinction is best described as:
choices: Damage to amygdala neurons over time
Erasure of the original fear trace
New learning that competes with the fear
Forgetting caused by the passage of time
test.explain: Extinction adds an inhibitory safety memory. The original fear memory survives, which is why fear can return.

test.q: Fear returns when a rat is tested in the original conditioning context after extinction elsewhere. This is called:
test.explain: Renewal is context-dependent return of fear, as in the ABA design. Reinstatement instead follows an unexpected aversive event.

test.q: Which region in rodents promotes extinction recall by calming amygdala output?
test.explain: Infralimbic cortex, similar to human vmPFC, drives inhibition in the amygdala. Prelimbic cortex tends to promote fear expression.

test.q: In Nader et al. (2000), anisomycin reduced later fear only when it was given:
choices: Without a reminder of the tone
Right after a reminder of the tone
test.explain: Blocking protein synthesis worked only after reactivation, showing the recalled memory had become labile and needed restabilizing.

test.q: What role does the hippocampus play in extinction?
choices: It encodes context that gates recall
It releases cortisol into the blood
test.explain: The hippocampus supplies context, determining whether the fear or the extinction memory wins.

test.q: Which condition appears necessary to destabilize a memory for reconsolidation?
test.explain: A mismatch between expectation and outcome triggers destabilization. Old, strong memories resist it, and long exposure shifts to extinction.

test.q: Exposure therapy for a spider phobia relies mainly on:
test.explain: Repeated safe contact with the feared cue builds extinction learning, much like CS-alone trials.

test.q: Why do therapists practice exposure in many settings?
test.explain: Extinction is context-bound, so varying contexts helps the safety memory generalize and reduces renewal.

test.q: D-cycloserine was studied for extinction because it acts on:
test.explain: Extinction consolidation needs NMDA receptors, and D-cycloserine is a partial NMDA agonist.

test.q: Fear that returns simply after time passes, without new training, is called spontaneous ___.
test.explain: Spontaneous recovery shows the original memory was suppressed, not erased.

test.q: What process restabilizes a memory after it is recalled and becomes labile?
test.explain: Reconsolidation requires new protein synthesis and offers a window for editing.

test.q: Fear returning after an unexpected unpleasant event is called ___.
test.explain: Reinstatement is one of three return-of-fear phenomena, alongside renewal and spontaneous recovery.

kidTest.q: What happens in extinction?
kidTest.explain: Fear fades because the brain learns that the cue is now safe.

kidTest.q: During extinction, the brain:
kidTest.explain: The old note stays, and a new "safe now" note is written on top.

kidTest.q: Why can an old fear sneak back?
choices: The brain grew a new part
The first note was still there
kidTest.explain: The old memory was never erased, so it can come back.

kidTest.q: Right after you remember something, the memory is:
kidTest.explain: For a short time it can change, like soft clay, before it hardens again.

kidTest.q: Fading of a fear when nothing bad happens is called e _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Extinction means the fear goes down with safe experiences.

advancedTest.q: A single brief reminder followed by propranolol reduces startle but leaves stated knowledge of the CS-US link intact. This best suggests:
choices: The reminder was long enough to produce new extinction learning
Propranolol is blocking the NMDA receptors needed for retrieval
The declarative memory was erased while the emotional one remained
Emotional and declarative components dissociate during restabilization
advancedTest.explain: Kindt's finding shows β-adrenergic blockade weakened the emotional expression while contingency knowledge survived. The last option reverses the result.

advancedTest.q: A lengthened reactivation session abolishes an anisomycin amnesic effect. The most likely explanation is:
choices: The memory became too old to destabilize
Prediction error was absent during retrieval
advancedTest.explain: Too much unreinforced exposure engages extinction instead of reconsolidation, so blocking restabilization no longer weakens the original trace.

advancedTest.q: Blocking GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors at retrieval would be expected to:
choices: Enhance destabilization, making anisomycin more effective
Prevent destabilization, protecting the memory from anisomycin
advancedTest.explain: GluN2B is needed to destabilize the memory. Without destabilization, protein synthesis inhibition has nothing labile to disrupt.

advancedTest.q: Return of fear after some amnesic manipulations is cited as evidence for:
advancedTest.explain: If an "erased" memory can return, the trace likely persisted but became hard to retrieve.

lessons.title: Dopamine and Reward Prediction Error

levels.kid:
Imagine you expect one cookie after dinner, but you get three. Wow! That is a happy surprise. If you expect a cookie and get nothing, you feel let down.

Deep inside your brain, a small group of cells makes a chemical messenger called **dopamine**. These cells work like a surprise meter:
- Better than you expected? They fire fast.
- Worse than you expected? They go quiet.
- Exactly what you expected? They hardly change.

Scientists call this a **reward prediction error**. It is the gap between what you expected and what you got.

Your brain uses that gap to learn. Next time, it makes a better guess. That is how you learn which things are worth trying again.
levels.hs:
**Dopamine** is a neurotransmitter made by a small group of neurons in the midbrain. Most are in the **ventral tegmental area (VTA)** and the **substantia nigra pars compacta**. Their axons reach the striatum and the prefrontal cortex.

People often call dopamine the "pleasure chemical," but that is misleading. In the 1990s, Wolfram Schultz recorded single dopamine neurons in monkeys that were given drops of juice. He found that the neurons signal a **reward prediction error (RPE)**:
- **Unexpected juice:** the neurons fire a burst. This is a positive error: better than expected.
- **Juice fully predicted by a light:** little change when the juice arrives.
- **Light shown but juice withheld:** firing dips below normal at the exact moment the juice was due. This is a negative error: worse than expected.

After learning, the burst moves to the light itself, because the light is now the earliest reliable sign of reward.

In short: **RPE = reward received - reward expected.**

This works as a teaching signal. Positive errors strengthen the cues and actions that led to the good surprise. Negative errors weaken them. Over many trials, expectations become more accurate and the errors shrink.

An everyday example: a phone notification sound may come to trigger a dopamine response by itself, because it predicts that something interesting could follow.
levels.college:
Midbrain dopamine neurons are few, roughly a few hundred thousand in humans, but they project widely:
- The **mesolimbic** pathway runs from the VTA to the nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum).
- The **mesocortical** pathway runs from the VTA to prefrontal cortex.
- The **nigrostriatal** pathway runs from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) to the dorsal striatum.

**Firing modes.**
- **Tonic** firing is a steady pacemaker rhythm of roughly 2-5 spikes per second. It maintains background dopamine levels.
- **Phasic** activity consists of bursts (about 15-30 Hz, lasting about 100-200 ms) or brief pauses. These occur with short latency, around 100 ms, after unexpected events.

**The RPE pattern.** Phasic responses track reward received minus reward predicted, and they scale with reward size and probability. After learning, they shift to the earliest predictive cue. A fully predicted reward evokes little response. An omitted reward produces a pause at the expected time.

**Link to learning theory.** The **Rescorla-Wagner** model (1972) proposed that surprise drives learning: associative strength changes in proportion to the error. This explains **blocking**. If cue A already predicts food, then pairing cue B with A produces little learning about B, because the food is no longer surprising. Dopamine neurons show blocking too. Schultz's data also matched **temporal-difference (TD) learning**, an algorithm from artificial intelligence that computes errors moment by moment.

**How the signal changes synapses.** In the striatum, dopamine acts as a "third factor." Corticostriatal synapses that were just active are strengthened or weakened depending on the dopamine signal.
- **D1** receptors (direct, "Go" pathway) have low affinity, so they are engaged mainly by bursts. This promotes potentiation that reinforces the chosen action.
- **D2** receptors (indirect, "NoGo" pathway) have high affinity, so they register the drop in dopamine during pauses. This favors learning to avoid poor choices.

**Wanting vs liking.** Kent Berridge's work suggests that dopamine drives **incentive salience**, or "wanting": the motivation to pursue a reward. Hedonic "liking" depends more on opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots in the accumbens and ventral pallidum.
levels.phd:
**Temporal-difference (TD) learning.** Schultz, Dayan and Montague (Science, 1997) showed that phasic dopamine matches the TD error of reinforcement learning: δ(t) = r(t) + γV(s(t+1)) - V(s(t)). Here V is the predicted sum of future reward and γ (between 0 and 1) discounts delayed reward.

Rescorla-Wagner computes one error per trial. TD instead computes errors continuously, and this explains why responses transfer to cues. A cue whose timing is itself unpredictable causes a jump in V, which produces a positive δ at cue onset. The reward, now predicted, yields δ close to zero. Omission yields a negative δ precisely when reward was due, so the circuit must encode timing.

**Quantitative properties.**
- **Probability:** Fiorillo, Tobler and Schultz (2003) found that cue responses rose, and reward responses fell, roughly linearly with reward probability. A separate sustained ramp peaked at p = 0.5, possibly reflecting uncertainty.
- **Adaptive coding:** Tobler, Fiorillo and Schultz (2005) showed that responses rescale to the range of rewards currently on offer, a form of gain control.
- **Asymmetry:** tonic rates are low, which leaves little room to decrease firing. Bayer and Glimcher (2005) found that rate coded positive errors well, while negative errors were better captured by pause duration.

**Causality.** Waelti, Dickinson and Schultz (2001) showed that dopamine neurons obey blocking. Steinberg et al. (2013) went further. They optogenetically stimulated rat VTA dopamine neurons at reward delivery during blocking training, and this "unblocked" learning about the redundant cue. Phasic dopamine is therefore sufficient to drive error-based learning.

**Computing the expectation.** Cohen et al. (2012) found that VTA GABA neurons show sustained activity during reward-predicting cues, encoding expectation. Eshel et al. (2015) showed that dopamine neurons subtract expectation arithmetically, and that manipulating VTA GABA neurons altered this subtraction.

**Heterogeneity and controversy.** Matsumoto and Hikosaka (2009) described dopamine neurons, concentrated in dorsolateral SNc, that were excited by both reward and aversive cues. This suggests that salience signals coexist with value coding. Berridge's group found that rats with near-total 6-OHDA dopamine depletion still show normal hedonic taste reactions to sucrose, yet will not work to obtain it. How this incentive-salience view maps onto RPE remains debated.
levels.expert:
**Measuring release, not just spikes.** Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and genetically encoded sensors (dLight, GRAB-DA) now track dopamine release in behaving animals. One surprise is that release and firing can dissociate. Mohebi et al. (2019) found that accumbens dopamine ramps up as rats approach reward, tracking value, without matching changes in VTA spiking. Local mechanisms, including cholinergic interneurons acting on dopamine axons, can evoke release independently of somatic firing. Approach ramps (Howe et al., 2013) are now interpreted either as value signals or as TD errors in a continuously changing state space.

**Distributional RL.** Dabney et al. (Nature, 2020) reported that mouse VTA neurons differ in their reversal points and in how steeply they scale positive versus negative errors. Optimistic cells, which amplify positive errors, settle at high quantiles of the reward distribution. Pessimistic cells settle at low quantiles. The population therefore encodes the shape of the distribution, not just its mean, mirroring a deep-RL method.

**Challenges to pure RPE.**
- Jeong, Namboodiri and colleagues (Science, 2022) argued that dopamine better fits ANCCR, a retrospective causal-learning signal that asks which cue preceded reward.
- Dopamine also carries identity and sensory prediction errors (Takahashi et al., 2017) and supports model-based learning without value (Sharpe et al., 2017).
- Movement and novelty signals in dorsal striatum make projection-specific heterogeneity the default assumption.

**Clinical translation.**
- **Parkinson's disease:** Frank et al. (2004) found that patients off medication learned better from negative feedback, and patients on medication learned better from positive feedback. This fits the idea that raised tonic dopamine fills in the dips that teach D2 NoGo cells.
- **Pharmacology in healthy volunteers:** Pessiglione et al. (2006) showed that L-DOPA enhanced striatal RPE signals and reward learning, whereas haloperidol reduced them.
- **Impulse control disorders:** D2/D3 agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole are linked to these disorders. In the DOMINION study, about 14% of treated Parkinson's patients had one.
- **Psychosis:** Kapur's aberrant salience hypothesis proposes that dysregulated dopamine assigns importance to irrelevant stimuli.
- **Addiction:** Redish (2004) modeled drugs that raise dopamine directly as producing an error that cannot be predicted away, so the learned value keeps growing.

**Pitfall.** Striatal fMRI "RPE" signals largely reflect synaptic input and local processing, not dopamine release itself.

keyPoints: Midbrain dopamine neurons (VTA, SNc) signal reward prediction errors
RPE = reward received minus reward expected
Better than expected: burst; worse: pause; as expected: little change
After learning, the burst moves to the earliest predictive cue
TD learning explains the pattern; phasic dopamine can causally drive learning
Dopamine drives 'wanting'; RPE coding informs Parkinson's, psychosis and addiction

test.q: Most dopamine neurons that signal reward prediction errors sit in which midbrain regions?
test.explain: The ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra pars compacta contain the dopamine neurons. The locus coeruleus and raphe nuclei make noradrenaline and serotonin instead.

test.q: A monkey receives juice it did not expect. Its dopamine neurons:
test.explain: An unexpected reward is better than predicted, which is a positive prediction error, so the neurons burst.

test.q: After a monkey learns that a light predicts juice, the dopamine burst occurs mainly at:
test.explain: The response transfers to the earliest reliable predictor of reward. The juice, now expected, evokes little response.

test.q: If a predicted reward is withheld, dopamine firing:
test.explain: Omission is worse than expected, so firing drops below baseline at the moment the reward should have arrived. This shows the system encodes timing.

test.q: Reward prediction error is best defined as:
choices: The delay between a cue and a reward
Total reward over a lifetime of trials
The pleasure felt while eating a reward
test.explain: RPE is the gap between what you got and what you predicted. It is not a measure of pleasure.

test.q: Berridge's work suggests dopamine is more closely tied to:
test.explain: Dopamine drives incentive salience, or wanting. Hedonic liking depends more on opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots.

test.q: Acting as a teaching signal, positive prediction errors tend to:
test.explain: Better-than-expected outcomes reinforce the cues and actions that led to them and raise expectations, so the error shrinks next time.

test.q: Low-affinity D1 receptors on direct-pathway striatal neurons are engaged mainly by:
test.explain: Low affinity means D1 receptors need high dopamine concentrations, which occur during bursts. High-affinity D2 receptors detect pauses.

test.q: Cue A already predicts food. When cue B is added alongside A, little is learned about B because:
choices: The added cue is too dim
test.explain: This is blocking. Food is already predicted by A, so there is no prediction error to drive learning about B.

test.q: Schultz's dopamine findings matched an AI algorithm called temporal-___ learning.
test.explain: Temporal-difference (TD) learning computes prediction errors moment by moment, which explains why responses shift to cues.

test.q: What three-letter abbreviation is used for reward prediction error?
test.explain: RPE stands for reward prediction error: reward received minus reward expected.

test.q: Dopamine neurons fire steadily at a few spikes per second; this background pattern is called ___ firing.
test.explain: Tonic firing maintains background dopamine. Phasic bursts and pauses carry the prediction-error signal.

kidTest.q: What do dopamine cells act like?
kidTest.explain: They measure how surprising something is: better or worse than you expected.

kidTest.q: You get MORE treats than you expected. Your dopamine cells:
kidTest.explain: A happy surprise makes dopamine cells fire fast.

kidTest.q: You expected a cookie but got nothing. Your dopamine cells:
kidTest.explain: When things are worse than expected, the cells go quiet.

kidTest.q: Why does the brain pay attention to surprises?
kidTest.explain: The surprise gap helps the brain learn, so it makes better guesses next time.

kidTest.q: The brain chemical that works like a surprise meter is d _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Dopamine cells fire when things are better than expected and go quiet when they are worse.

advancedTest.q: In a TD model, δ = r + γV(s') - V(s). Why does the dopamine burst move to the cue after learning?
choices: The cue becomes rewarding through sensitization
Reward value decays to zero once the cue is learned
Dopamine neurons habituate to the juice's taste
Cue onset is unpredicted and raises expected value
advancedTest.explain: The cue arrives at an unpredictable time and causes a jump in V, which produces a positive δ. The reward is now predicted, so its δ is near zero. Its value has not disappeared.

advancedTest.q: Optogenetically driving VTA dopamine neurons at reward delivery during blocking training lets rats learn about the redundant cue. This shows that:
choices: Phasic dopamine can causally drive learning
Blocking depends on attention, not prediction
The laser light acts as an unexpected reward
Dopamine merely tracks errors computed elsewhere
advancedTest.explain: Steinberg et al. (2013) unblocked learning by artificially supplying the missing error signal. This shows dopamine is sufficient to drive learning, not just correlated with it.

advancedTest.q: In distributional RL, a dopamine neuron that scales positive errors more steeply than negative ones will come to encode:
choices: The mean reward, as in classic TD learning
advancedTest.explain: Amplifying positive errors pushes the neuron's equilibrium upward, toward high quantiles. Across many such neurons, the population encodes the whole reward distribution, as Dabney et al. (2020) reported.

advancedTest.q: Why might Parkinson's patients on dopaminergic medication learn worse from negative outcomes?
choices: The drugs block D1 receptors on direct-pathway cells
Higher tonic dopamine masks teaching dips
The drugs kill the surviving nigral neurons
advancedTest.explain: Negative learning relies on high-affinity D2 receptors detecting dopamine dips. Elevated tonic dopamine fills in those dips, which fits the findings of Frank et al. (2004).

lessons.title: Stress, the HPA Axis and Cognitive Performance

levels.kid:
Imagine a big dog suddenly barks at you. Your heart pounds and you feel ready to run. That is your body's **stress alarm**.

The alarm works like a relay race. A brain part called the **hypothalamus** passes a message to the **pituitary**, a gland about the size of a pea. The pituitary sends a signal through your blood to the **adrenal glands**, which sit just above your kidneys. They make a hormone called **cortisol**.

A medium amount of stress helps you focus, like right before a race. Too much makes your thinking go fuzzy, so you might blank on a test. If stress lasts for weeks, it can wear out the **hippocampus**, your brain's memory helper.

Sleep, exercise, slow breathing and talking to someone you trust all help switch the alarm off.
levels.hs:
When you face a threat, your body runs two stress systems.

The fast one is the **sympathetic nervous system**. Within seconds, the adrenal medulla releases **adrenaline**, and a tiny brainstem nucleus called the **locus coeruleus** floods the brain with **noradrenaline**. Your heart speeds up and you become alert.

The slower one is the **HPA axis** (hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal):
- The **hypothalamus** releases **CRH** (corticotropin-releasing hormone).
- The **anterior pituitary** responds by releasing **ACTH** into the blood.
- The **adrenal cortex** makes **cortisol**, which peaks roughly 15–30 minutes after a stressor begins.

Cortisol raises blood sugar and also acts on the brain. It then limits its own release by **negative feedback** on the brain and pituitary, like a thermostat.

Stress and performance follow an **inverted U** (the Yerkes–Dodson pattern). Moderate arousal sharpens focus, but high arousal takes the **prefrontal cortex**, which holds information in working memory, partly offline. That is one reason you can blank on a test you studied for: high cortisol makes it harder to **retrieve** memories, even though stress hormones released just after an event help **store** it.

Real example: in the **Trier Social Stress Test**, volunteers give a surprise speech and do mental math in front of stern judges, which reliably raises cortisol.

When stress becomes chronic, the cumulative wear and tear on the body and brain is called **allostatic load**.
levels.college:
**Two arms of the stress response.** The sympathetic–adrenomedullary (SAM) system acts in seconds: adrenaline from the adrenal medulla and noradrenaline from the **locus coeruleus (LC)** raise arousal. The HPA axis acts over minutes. Parvocellular neurons of the hypothalamic **paraventricular nucleus (PVN)** release **CRH** (with vasopressin) into the hypophyseal portal veins. Pituitary corticotrophs cleave pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) to release **ACTH**, which drives the adrenal **zona fasciculata** to secrete **cortisol** (corticosterone in rodents).

**Control.** Cortisol follows a circadian rhythm, peaking shortly after waking (the **cortisol awakening response**). Negative feedback operates at the pituitary, PVN and hippocampus, while the amygdala drives CRH output. Glucocorticoids act through two receptors:
- **MR** (mineralocorticoid receptor): high affinity, largely occupied at baseline.
- **GR** (glucocorticoid receptor): lower affinity, recruited at stress and circadian peaks.
Both are ligand-activated transcription factors, so many effects unfold over hours.

**Cognitive effects of acute stress.**
- **Prefrontal cortex**: high noradrenaline and dopamine impair working memory and flexible control (inverted U).
- **Consolidation**: stress hormones around learning strengthen storage of emotionally arousing events, via noradrenaline in the **basolateral amygdala (BLA)**.
- **Retrieval**: high cortisol at test impairs recall of previously learned material.
- **Strategy shift**: stress biases behavior away from hippocampus- and PFC-dependent goal-directed strategies toward **dorsal striatum**–dependent habits.

**Chronic stress.** In rodents, weeks of stress cause dendritic retraction in hippocampal CA3 and medial PFC, reduced neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus, and dendritic growth in the BLA. The brain becomes more reactive and less flexible. McEwen's concept of **allostasis** (stability through change) frames this: the response is adaptive short term, but cumulative **allostatic load** contributes to disease.
levels.phd:
**Receptor logic.** De Kloet's two-receptor model explains biphasic glucocorticoid effects. MR binds cortisol with roughly tenfold higher affinity than GR, so MR is near-saturated at basal levels and supports tonic excitability and appraisal, whereas GR fills during stress and circadian peaks, terminating the response and promoting recovery. The MR:GR balance, not hormone level alone, predicts outcome, giving one mechanistic basis for inverted-U curves. Beyond genomic actions, membrane-associated receptors act within minutes: membrane MR raises glutamate release probability in hippocampus, and in the PVN glucocorticoids trigger retrograde endocannabinoid signaling that suppresses glutamatergic drive (Tasker), a fast feedback route.

**Prefrontal collapse.** Arnsten showed that persistent delay-period firing in layer III recurrent PFC microcircuits depends on catecholamine level. Moderate noradrenaline at **α2A receptors** on spines inhibits cAMP, closing **HCN** and **KCNQ** channels and strengthening network connectivity. Stress-level release engages α1 and β receptors and excess D1 stimulation, raising cAMP–PKA and PKC signaling, opening those channels and silencing persistent firing. Chronic stress adds apical dendritic spine loss in medial PFC (Radley, Morrison), reversible in young animals but less so with age.

**Memory modulation.** In McGaugh's model, arousal releases noradrenaline in the BLA, which projects to hippocampus, striatum and cortex to boost consolidation; glucocorticoid enhancement requires intact BLA β-adrenergic signaling (Roozendaal). Cahill and colleagues (1994) found that propranolol given before an emotional story abolished the memory advantage for its emotional segment while sparing the neutral one. De Quervain (rats 1998, humans 2000) showed glucocorticoids at test impair retrieval: the hormone that helps storage hurts recall.

**Systems switch.** Schwabe and Wolf showed that stress before instrumental training renders behavior insensitive to outcome devaluation, an MR- and noradrenaline-dependent shift to striatal habit.

**Nuance.** Yerkes and Dodson (1908) studied mice learning a discrimination under shocks of varying strength; the general arousal–performance law is a later reinterpretation, and many inverted-U claims are post hoc. Controllability matters too: Maier showed that perceived control engages medial PFC to inhibit the dorsal raphe, protecting against learned helplessness.
levels.expert:
**Clinical hypercortisolism.** **Cushing's syndrome** is a natural experiment: patients show memory and mood impairment and reduced hippocampal volume that partly recovers once cortisol normalizes (Starkman). For neurosurgeons, **Cushing's disease** (an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) is treated by transsphenoidal resection; a very low postoperative cortisol signals likely remission, and patients need glucocorticoid replacement while the suppressed axis recovers. Exogenous glucocorticoids, such as dexamethasone for peritumoral vasogenic edema, can cause insomnia, mood swings, memory complaints and occasionally psychosis, which matters when assessing postoperative cognition.

**Depression and PTSD.** Carroll's **dexamethasone suppression test** revealed nonsuppression in many patients with melancholic depression, implying impaired GR feedback, but it proved too nonspecific for diagnosis. PTSD often shows the opposite profile: normal or low basal cortisol with enhanced feedback sensitivity (Yehuda). Studies of hydrocortisone given during septic shock or cardiac surgery (Schelling) found fewer later traumatic memories and PTSD symptoms, plausibly by dampening retrieval of traumatic memories.

**Translational failures.** CRH-R1 antagonists (pexacerfont, verucerfont) failed in depression, anxiety and alcohol-use trials, and the GR antagonist mifepristone gave mixed results in psychotic depression. The axis is a hub; blocking one node rarely fixes a network-level problem.

**Gene × environment.** Rat pups of high licking/grooming mothers had less methylation of the hippocampal GR promoter, more GR and calmer stress responses (Weaver, Meaney 2004); McGowan (2009) found related changes in hippocampus from suicide victims with childhood abuse. **FKBP5**, a GR co-chaperone that lowers GR sensitivity, interacts with childhood trauma to predict PTSD risk (Binder 2008), partly through trauma-linked demethylation (Klengel 2013).

**Measurement pitfalls.**
- Cortisol swings across the day, so sampling time must be fixed.
- Salivary cortisol reflects free hormone; oral contraceptives raise binding globulin and blunt salivary stress responses.
- Hair cortisol indexes months, not moments.
- Many studies confound cortisol with catecholamine effects.

**Open questions.** Can GR or FKBP5 modulators restore cognitive flexibility without systemic side effects? Why do some brains remodel back after stress while others stay locked in a reactive state?

keyPoints: The HPA axis runs hypothalamus (CRH) to pituitary (ACTH) to adrenal cortex (cortisol)
Cortisol limits its own release by negative feedback via GR in brain and pituitary
Stress and performance follow an inverted U; high catecholamines take the PFC offline
Stress hormones strengthen memory storage but impair retrieval at test
Acute stress shifts behavior from goal-directed control toward striatal habits
Chronic stress shrinks hippocampal and PFC dendrites, grows amygdala dendrites: allostatic load

test.q: What is the correct order of signaling in the HPA axis?
test.explain: The hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex makes cortisol. The adrenal medulla belongs to the fast sympathetic arm, not the HPA axis.

test.q: Which hormone does the anterior pituitary release to stimulate cortisol production?
test.explain: ACTH travels in the blood to the adrenal cortex. CRH comes from the hypothalamus one step earlier.

test.q: Cortisol limits its own release mainly through:
choices: Positive feedback on the adrenal medulla
Negative feedback on brain and pituitary
Breakdown of ACTH within the bloodstream
test.explain: Like a thermostat, cortisol acts on GR in the pituitary, hypothalamus and hippocampus to turn down CRH and ACTH release.

test.q: The inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance predicts that:
choices: Low arousal yields the best performance
Performance rises steadily as arousal increases
Moderate arousal yields the best performance
Performance is unrelated to arousal level
test.explain: Performance peaks at moderate arousal and falls off when arousal is too low or too high.

test.q: Which region, critical for working memory, is partly taken offline by high catecholamine levels during acute stress?
test.explain: High noradrenaline and dopamine weaken prefrontal working-memory activity. The dorsal striatum, by contrast, gains influence under stress.

test.q: In rodent studies, chronic stress tends to:
choices: Shrink dendrites in both the hippocampus and the amygdala
Shrink hippocampal dendrites and grow amygdala dendrites
Grow hippocampal dendrites and shrink amygdala dendrites
Grow dendrites in both the hippocampus and the amygdala
test.explain: Chronic stress causes dendritic retraction in hippocampal CA3 and medial PFC but dendritic growth in the basolateral amygdala, making the brain more reactive and less flexible.

test.q: Stress hormones released shortly after an emotional event tend to:
choices: Leave memory of the event unchanged
Block encoding of the earlier event
Erase the memory within a few hours
test.explain: Noradrenaline in the basolateral amygdala, aided by cortisol, enhances consolidation of emotionally arousing memories.

test.q: A student with very high cortisol right before an exam is most likely to have trouble with:
test.explain: High cortisol at the time of testing impairs retrieval of previously learned material, which is why people can blank on material they know.

test.q: Under stress, people tend to shift from flexible goal-directed behavior toward:
choices: Spatial maps supported by the hippocampus
Habits supported by the dorsal striatum
Planning supported by the prefrontal cortex
test.explain: Stress biases control away from hippocampal and prefrontal strategies toward dorsal striatum habits.

test.q: Which steroid hormone is the main end product of the human HPA axis?
test.explain: The adrenal cortex secretes cortisol in humans; rodents use corticosterone.

test.q: The cumulative wear and tear on the body and brain from chronic stress is called allostatic ___.
test.explain: Allostatic load, a concept developed by McEwen, describes the cost of repeated or prolonged stress responses.

test.q: Which small brainstem nucleus is the brain's main source of noradrenaline during the fast stress response?
test.explain: The locus coeruleus releases noradrenaline widely across the brain within seconds of a threat.

kidTest.q: Where are the adrenal glands?
kidTest.explain: The adrenal glands sit just above your kidneys and make cortisol.

kidTest.q: How much stress helps you do your best?
kidTest.explain: A medium amount helps you focus. Too much makes thinking fuzzy.

kidTest.q: Which memory helper in the brain can get worn out by stress that lasts for weeks?
kidTest.explain: The hippocampus helps make memories, and long-lasting stress can wear it out.

kidTest.q: Which is a good way to switch off the stress alarm?
kidTest.explain: Sleep helps your body calm the stress alarm. Skipping sleep makes stress worse.

kidTest.q: The stress hormone made by the adrenal glands is called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Cortisol is the stress hormone at the end of the relay race.

advancedTest.q: Why is GR occupancy, rather than MR occupancy, thought to drive feedback termination of the HPA response?
choices: MR is found mainly in the adrenal cortex rather than the brain
MR binds ACTH rather than cortisol, so it ignores cortisol
GR has lower affinity, so it fills mainly when cortisol is high
GR has higher affinity, so it is saturated at basal cortisol
advancedTest.explain: MR binds cortisol with about tenfold higher affinity and is near-saturated at baseline, so changes in feedback during peaks depend on the lower-affinity GR filling up.

advancedTest.q: Based on Arnsten's model, a drug that stimulates alpha-2A adrenoceptors on PFC dendritic spines would be predicted to:
choices: Weaken persistent firing by raising PKA activity
Weaken persistent firing by opening HCN channels
Strengthen persistent firing by blocking glutamate receptors
Strengthen persistent firing by reducing cAMP signaling
advancedTest.explain: Alpha-2A signaling inhibits cAMP, closing HCN and KCNQ channels and strengthening recurrent network firing. Blocking glutamate receptors would weaken, not strengthen, these circuits.

advancedTest.q: Propranolol given before an emotional story removes the memory advantage for its emotional part but spares memory for the neutral part. This best supports the idea that:
choices: Cortisol acts directly on beta receptors to block storage
Noradrenergic beta signaling boosts emotional memory storage
Emotional memories rely on the cerebellum rather than the amygdala
Propranolol broadly impairs hippocampal encoding of any material
advancedTest.explain: Selective loss of the emotional enhancement, with neutral memory intact, points to beta-adrenergic modulation (in the BLA) rather than a general encoding deficit.

advancedTest.q: Cortisol given right after learning improves later recall, yet cortisol given just before a test impairs recall. The best explanation is that:
choices: Glucocorticoids aid retrieval but impair consolidation
Cortisol is broken down too fast to act before a test
Post-learning cortisol works by raising test motivation
Glucocorticoids aid consolidation but impair retrieval
advancedTest.explain: De Quervain's studies show a timing dissociation: the same hormone enhances storage after learning but disrupts retrieval at test.

lessons.title: Interoception, the Insula and the Feeling of Emotion

levels.kid:
Close your eyes and sit very still. Can you feel your heart thumping? Your tummy rumbling? Your breath going in and out? Feeling what is happening inside your body has a big name: **interoception** (say it: in-ter-oh-SEP-shun).

Tiny messenger nerves carry news from your heart, lungs and tummy up to your brain. A hidden part of the brain called the **insula** reads that news. It is like a reporter writing a daily report about your insides.

Your feelings use this report too! When you are scared, your heart races. When you are nervous, you get butterflies in your tummy. Your brain notices these body signals and helps turn them into the feeling of being scared or nervous.
levels.hs:
**Interoception** is your sense of the body's internal state: heartbeat, breathing, hunger, thirst, temperature, a full bladder, nausea. It is a sense just like sight or hearing, except the signals come from inside you.

How the signals travel:
- The **vagus nerve** carries messages from the heart, lungs and gut to the brainstem.
- Small nerve fibers in the spinal cord carry signals about pain, temperature and itch.
- These pathways relay through the brainstem and thalamus to the **insula**, a fold of cortex tucked deep inside the lateral sulcus, the big groove on the side of the brain.

Why does this matter for emotion? In the 1880s William James argued that emotions are partly the feeling of bodily changes. We don't just tremble because we are afraid; feeling ourselves tremble is part of being afraid. Modern research supports a version of this idea: the brain combines body signals with knowledge of the situation to build an emotional experience.

A real example: in a **heartbeat detection task**, people try to sense their own heartbeats without touching their pulse. Some are accurate, others are not. In a well-known 2004 brain-imaging study, people who were better at sensing their heartbeat showed more activity in the **right anterior (front) insula**, and they tended to report stronger bodily feelings and more anxiety.
levels.college:
Interoception is the sensing, integration and interpretation of signals about the body's physiological condition. It supports homeostasis and, many researchers argue, the felt quality of emotion.

**Afferent pathways.**
- **Vagal and glossopharyngeal afferents** (cardiac baroreceptors, lung stretch receptors, gut mechano- and chemoreceptors) end in the **nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS)** in the medulla.
- **Lamina I spinothalamic neurons** in the dorsal horn carry small-fiber signals: pain, temperature, itch, muscle burn, gentle affective touch.
- Both streams reach the **parabrachial nucleus** and the thalamus (ventromedial posterior and basal ventromedial nuclei), then the **dorsal posterior insula**, often called primary interoceptive cortex.

**A posterior-to-anterior gradient.** In A. D. (Bud) Craig's model, the posterior insula represents raw physiological signals, the mid insula integrates them with other senses and motivational context, and the **anterior insula** forms a higher-order representation of how the body feels right now, which Craig linked to subjective awareness. The anterior insula works closely with the **anterior cingulate cortex (ACC)**: the insula as the 'feeling' end, the ACC as the 'motivation and action' end.

**Emotion theories.**
- **James-Lange**: emotion is the perception of bodily change.
- **Cannon-Bard** objected that visceral responses are too slow and too similar across emotions, proposing thalamic signals that trigger feeling and body response in parallel.
- **Schachter-Singer**: physiological arousal plus a cognitive label produces emotion.
- **Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis**: body-state signals, mapped in insula and somatosensory cortex and linked to ventromedial prefrontal cortex, bias decisions.

**Evidence linking insula and feeling.**
- Anterior insula activates during disgust, both felt and seen in others' faces.
- It activates when we feel pain and when we watch a loved one receive pain (Singer, 2004).
- Smokers whose strokes damaged the insula were far more likely to quit easily, without strong urges (Naqvi, 2007).

The anterior insula and dorsal ACC form the core of the **salience network**, which flags events that matter and helps switch the brain between inward-focused and task-focused modes.
levels.phd:
Measurement is the field's central problem. The **heartbeat counting task** (Schandry, 1981) is confounded by knowledge of one's typical heart rate; many high scorers are estimating, not sensing. **Heartbeat discrimination** tasks (judging whether tones are synchronous with one's heartbeat) resist this but yield near-chance performance in most people. Garfinkel and colleagues (2015) separated three dimensions: **interoceptive accuracy** (objective performance), **interoceptive sensibility** (self-reported belief about one's body awareness), and **interoceptive awareness**, the metacognitive match between confidence and accuracy. These dissociate: in autism, for example, sensibility can be high while accuracy is low.

**Cardiac timing** offers an implicit probe. Arterial baroreceptors fire in bursts during systole, and this phasic input modulates processing: fearful faces are detected more readily and rated as more intense at systole than at diastole (Garfinkel et al., 2014), while pain and some simple stimuli are dampened at systole. The **heartbeat-evoked potential (HEP)**, an EEG/MEG deflection time-locked to the R-wave, indexes cortical processing of cardiac afferents and grows with attention to the body.

**Predictive processing** reframes interoception as inference. In models from Seth and from Barrett and Simmons (**EPIC**: Embodied Predictive Interoception Coding), agranular visceromotor cortices (anterior insula, ACC, orbitofrontal cortex) issue predictions about bodily states, and granular posterior insula compares them with incoming afferents to compute prediction errors. Feelings then reflect the brain's best guess about the causes of body signals, and regulation (**allostasis**) is anticipatory rather than reactive. Barrett's **theory of constructed emotion** extends this: emotion categories are built from interoceptive predictions plus learned concepts, not released by dedicated circuits.

**Lesion evidence complicates simple models.** Patient Roger (Khalsa et al., 2009), with near-complete bilateral insula destruction from herpes simplex encephalitis, retained heartbeat awareness and emotional feeling. When the skin over his chest was anesthetized, his heartbeat perception during adrenergic stimulation fell, implicating cutaneous afferents to somatosensory cortex. Interoceptive awareness is therefore distributed, and the insula's necessity for feeling remains contested, as does Craig's proposed right-sympathetic, left-parasympathetic lateralization.

The anterior insula and ACC also contain **von Economo neurons**, large spindle-shaped projection cells enriched in humans and great apes and depleted early in behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia.
levels.expert:
**Neurosurgical anatomy.** The insula lies beneath the frontal, temporal and parietal opercula, draped by M2 branches of the middle cerebral artery; medially it approaches the extreme and external capsules, claustrum and lenticulostriate territory. Insular gliomas, often lower grade, are reached transsylvian or transcortically. The Berger-Sanai classification divides the insula into four zones using the sylvian fissure and a perpendicular line through the foramen of Monro to predict extent of resection. The main hazard is ischemia from injury to perforators and long insular arteries, not loss of insular cortex itself; awake language and motor mapping is standard in dominant-hemisphere cases.

**Epilepsy.** Insular-opercular seizures masquerade as temporal, frontal or parietal epilepsy: laryngeal constriction, perioral paresthesias, epigastric rising sensations, hypersalivation, hypermotor behavior. Scalp EEG often misses them, so stereo-EEG sampling of the insula is routine when evaluating nonlesional cases. Direct stimulation (Penfield; later Isnard, Mazzola and the Lyon group) evokes visceral, somatosensory, gustatory and painful sensations. Rare 'ecstatic' seizures, with bliss and a sense of certainty, localize to dorsal anterior insula.

**Brain-heart coupling.** Insular infarction, right-sided in several series, is linked to arrhythmias, QT prolongation, troponin release and blood-pressure lability, part of the stroke-heart syndrome worth monitoring after MCA strokes.

**Psychiatry and interventions.** Altered interoception appears across panic, depression, anorexia nervosa, addiction and functional disorders. Khalsa's group uses bolus infusions of the beta-agonist isoproterenol to perturb heart rate transdiagnostically; patients often show exaggerated anticipatory anxiety and atypical insula responses. Heartbeat-discrimination training with feedback (the ADIE trial, Garfinkel and colleagues) reduced anxiety in autistic adults. Floatation-REST is being tested to sharpen interoceptive attention.

**Circuit-level advances.** Liberles and colleagues mapped genetically defined vagal sensory neurons, such as GLP1R-expressing gut stretch receptors, and showed that Piezo1/Piezo2 are required for baroreception. In mice, insular neurons encode hunger and thirst and, after food cues, shift toward representing the predicted future physiological state (Livneh, Andermann and colleagues, 2020), directly supporting predictive accounts.

**Open questions:** whether interoceptive accuracy is one trait or many channel-specific abilities; how insula-cingulate dynamics yield subjective feeling; and whether retraining interoception changes psychiatric outcomes durably.

keyPoints: Interoception is sensing the body's internal state: heartbeat, breath, gut, temperature
Vagal afferents reach the NTS; lamina I spinothalamic fibers carry pain, temperature and itch
Signals flow from posterior insula (raw) to anterior insula (felt state), partnered with ACC
James-Lange, somatic markers and predictive models tie emotion to body signals
Interoceptive accuracy, sensibility and awareness are separate, dissociable dimensions
Insula matters clinically: gliomas, insular seizures, cardiac effects of insular stroke

test.q: What is interoception?
choices: Sensing the position of the limbs
test.explain: Interoception covers internal signals like heartbeat, breathing, hunger and temperature. Limb position is proprioception, which is a different sense.

test.q: Where is the insula located?
choices: At the tip of the occipital lobe
On the top of the parietal lobe
Along the midline of the brainstem
test.explain: The insula is a fold of cortex hidden deep in the lateral (sylvian) sulcus, covered by the opercula of nearby lobes.

test.q: Which nerve carries signals from the heart, lungs and gut to the brainstem?
test.explain: The vagus nerve carries most visceral sensory signals from the chest and abdomen to the brainstem.

test.q: Vagal afferents first terminate in which structure?
choices: Dorsal horn of the cervical spinal cord
test.explain: Vagal and glossopharyngeal afferents end in the nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) in the medulla, which relays onward to parabrachial nucleus and thalamus.

test.q: In Craig's model, which region forms the highest-order representation of how the body feels?
test.explain: Craig proposed a posterior-to-anterior gradient: the posterior insula holds raw signals, and the anterior insula builds the integrated, felt body state.

test.q: The James-Lange theory holds that:
choices: Emotion arises before any bodily change
Emotion comes from thalamic signals to cortex
Emotion is a cognitive label with no arousal
Emotion is the perception of bodily change
test.explain: James and Lange argued that feeling the body's changes is the emotion. Thalamic triggering of feeling and body response in parallel is the Cannon-Bard view.

test.q: Naqvi (2007) found that smokers whose strokes damaged the insula:
choices: Smoked more heavily after the stroke
Lost their sense of smell for smoke
test.explain: Insula damage made quitting far easier and urges weaker, suggesting the insula helps represent the bodily feeling of craving.

test.q: The core of the salience network is formed by:
test.explain: The anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex flag important events and help switch between inward-focused and task-focused brain modes.

test.q: In the 2004 heartbeat-detection imaging study, better heartbeat sensing went with greater activity in the:
test.explain: People who sensed their heartbeat more accurately showed more right anterior insula activity and reported stronger bodily feelings and more anxiety.

test.q: Damasio's ___ marker hypothesis proposes that body-state signals bias decisions.
test.explain: Somatic markers are body-state signals, mapped in insula and somatosensory cortex and linked to ventromedial prefrontal cortex, that steer choices.

test.q: Which cortex partners with the anterior insula and is described as the 'motivation and action' end of the pair?
test.explain: The insula is the 'feeling' end and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) the 'motivation and action' end of this partnership.

test.q: Pain, temperature and itch signals travel in lamina ___ spinothalamic neurons of the dorsal horn.
test.explain: Lamina I neurons carry small-fiber signals about the body's condition toward the thalamus and insula.

kidTest.q: What does interoception mean?
choices: Feeling what goes on inside your body
Seeing bright colors that are far away
Hearing songs and sounds with your ears
kidTest.explain: Interoception is feeling your insides, like your heartbeat and a rumbling tummy.

kidTest.q: What hidden part of you reads the news from inside your body?
kidTest.explain: The insula is a hidden part of the brain that reads messages from your heart, lungs and tummy.

kidTest.q: When you are scared, what does your heart often do?
choices: It stops for a little while
kidTest.explain: Fear makes your heart race, and your brain notices this body signal.

kidTest.q: What can 'butterflies in your tummy' be a sign of?
kidTest.explain: Butterflies in your tummy are a body signal that often comes with feeling nervous.

kidTest.q: Feeling what happens inside your body has a big name: i _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Interoception means sensing your insides, like your heartbeat and breathing.

advancedTest.q: Patient Roger kept heartbeat awareness despite bilateral insula destruction, but it fell when his chest skin was anesthetized. The best inference is:
choices: Heartbeat sensing can use skin routes to somatosensory cortex
Heartbeat reports in Roger were guesses from his known heart rate
Heartbeat sensing arises in the brainstem without any cortex
Heartbeat sensing requires an intact posterior and anterior insula
advancedTest.explain: Losing perception when cutaneous input was blocked points to skin afferents reaching somatosensory cortex as an alternative route. His intact awareness rules out strict insula necessity.

advancedTest.q: An autistic adult reports strong body awareness on questionnaires but performs at chance on heartbeat discrimination. In Garfinkel's framework this is:
advancedTest.explain: Self-report is sensibility and task performance is accuracy; here they dissociate, as described in autism.

advancedTest.q: Fearful faces are rated more intense when shown at systole than at diastole. The most direct mechanistic explanation is:
choices: Attention to the heartbeat peaks during diastole
Eye movements are suppressed during each diastole
Visual cortex receives extra blood flow at systole
advancedTest.explain: Arterial baroreceptors fire phasically at systole, and this cardiac afferent signal modulates processing of threat cues, which is why timing relative to the heartbeat matters.

advancedTest.q: In the EPIC model, agranular visceromotor cortex predicts a rise in heart rate that does not occur. Where is the mismatch computed?
advancedTest.explain: Agranular regions such as anterior insula send predictions; granular posterior insula compares them with incoming afferents and computes the prediction error.
